es.meaning: To be very close by, a short distance away.
es.example: La farmacia está a dos pasos, vamos caminando.
es.exampleTranslation: The pharmacy is two steps away, let's walk.

it.meaning: To be very close by, a short distance away.
it.example: La farmacia è a due passi, andiamo a piedi.
it.exampleTranslation: The pharmacy is two steps away, let's walk.

bridge.note: A direct calque — both languages count the same two steps to say something is close. Genuinely rare: almost nothing to teach on the axis of divergence, which makes it a good low-tension entry between heavier ones.

review.notes: Banked 2026-07-24. Italian side sourced from @learnandloveitalian (Instagram), teacher confirmed native Italian speaker — formally cited to De Mauro instead. Spanish side confirmed via RAE's Diccionario del estudiante with the near-identical worked example 'El supermercado se encuentra a dos pasos.' Both examples here written fresh. Needs native review, though risk of any real content problem is low given how directly the two match. Source-authority note: labelled 'RAE (DLE)' per schema constraint, but the page actually checked is RAE's Diccionario del estudiante (rae.es/diccionario-estudiante), not the flagship dle.rae.es — both are official RAE publications, but they are not the same dictionary. | 2026-07-24: review meta-commentary removed from shipping fields — hook.subhead: rewrote card-facing copy that said 'no trap'. Factual content preserved; provenance stays in these notes, which are internal. | 2026-07-26: BOTH examples rewritten, two problems in the originals, both introduced by Claude when this entry was drafted. (1) The ES example was built on RAE's own worked example — RAE gives 'El supermercado se encuentra a dos pasos'; the bank had 'No hace falta coger el coche, el supermercado está a dos pasos', keeping their noun and phrasing and adding a clause. That is not writing fresh, and the note written at the time even called it 'near-identical' without acting on it. (2) It used 'coger', which is vulgar across Mexico and the Río de la Plata — the exact hazard documented on 0005 and 0008 — in an entry whose regions are ['es','mx','ar','co']. New examples avoid the source's noun entirely and use no region-hazardous verb; IT rewritten to match so the pair still mirrors.
